Nxeon VPS/game-server hosting platform, Next.js/TypeScript/Prisma/Postgres, repo /opt/nxeon (git, branch `main`), single Proxmox host, real production system.

## Context — why this matters

Two real, separate customer-facing bugs shipped silently today because PROVISION reports `DONE` based on "no API call threw an error," never "the customer can actually reach what got built":

1. A customer's game server got assigned an IP that was already in use by unrelated infrastructure (a networking-layer collision) — the VM existed, Proxmox accepted the config, but nothing was ever reachable.
2. Separately, EVERY game family's Docker-based setup script (`docker run -d ...`) creates no systemd unit, so the game software can silently fail to start correctly (confirmed: Terraria hung on an interactive world-selection menu with no TTY, so the container showed "Up" while the actual game server never bound its port) — again, PROVISION reported success.

Both would have been caught immediately by one real end-to-end check: after everything else in PROVISION finishes, actually try to reach the server the way a customer would, before ever telling anyone it's ready.

## What to build

In `worker/index.ts`'s `provision()` function (the `PROVISION` job handler — read the whole function first, it's long; the guest-agent-wait / readiness-message logic near the end, mentioned in a comment around "the hypervisor started the VM, but its guest agent has not answered yet," is the right area to extend), add a real health-verification step after the VM is confirmed started and before the server is marked ready / the "your server is ready" email is sent:

1. **SSH reachability** (applies to every server, VPS and game): a real TCP connect to the server's actual reachable address (dedicated IP if one was allocated, else the NAT'd host IP + assigned SSH port — check how `dedicated`/`ip`/`sshPort` are already computed earlier in this same function and reuse those, don't recompute) on port 22 (or the assigned SSH port for NAT servers), confirming an actual SSH banner comes back (`SSH-2.0-...`), not just that the TCP handshake completes — a closed port dropping the connection can look different from a real refusal, get the actual banner as proof.

2. **Game-specific port check** (only for game servers — check `server.gameVariant`/`server.gamePlan` to know if this is one): figure out the expected game port for this server (check `GamePlan`/`lib/game-config.ts`/`lib/games.ts` for where a game's actual listen port is defined — Terraria is 7777, others vary; find the real per-game port source rather than hardcoding one value) and do a real TCP connect to it. A game server takes longer to actually start listening than SSH does (image pull, world generation, etc.) — this check needs a genuine retry/backoff window, not a single immediate attempt: something like retrying every 5-10 seconds for a few minutes total is reasonable, tune based on what feels right once you see how long a real Terraria boot actually takes in this environment (you can test empirically against a real order if you place one, or reuse timing evidence from today's incident report if you have it).

3. **On failure**: after retries are exhausted, do NOT report the server as ready. Follow the existing failure-handling convention already in this function (there's clearly an established pattern for a failed PROVISION — status flips to `ERROR`, `provisionError` gets a clear human-readable message, the dedicated IP gets released back to the pool per the cleanup logic mentioned in `worker/index.ts` around "A terminally-failed PROVISION must not leak its allocated dedicated IP" — read that code and match it exactly). The error message should be genuinely diagnostic: e.g. "SSH did not respond after Ns" vs "game port 7777 never opened after Ns" — different messages for different failure points, since these point at different root causes for whoever investigates. The server-deployed email must never fire if this check fails.

4. **On success**: proceed exactly as today (server marked RUNNING, ready email sent, etc.) — no other behavior change.

## Ground rules

- Read the FULL `provision()` function before changing anything — it's long, has careful existing error-handling/idempotency/cleanup logic (PROVISION is designed to be safely re-runnable on retry), and your addition needs to fit that design, not fight it. In particular: if PROVISION is retried after this new health check fails and flips status to ERROR, make sure a subsequent retry can still succeed cleanly (the function already handles `vmAlreadyExists` idempotently — your health check should just re-run on a retry, not assume it's the first attempt).
- Don't touch anything about the actual Terraria world-hang bug or the missing-systemd-unit issue — those are separate, already-diagnosed problems being handled elsewhere (one already has a fix committed on `hotfix/game-install-gap`, not yet deployed; a Terraria `OsTemplate.setupScript` data fix already landed in the live DB). Your job is purely the verification step, not fixing what it verifies.
- Add real test coverage for anything cleanly separable into pure logic (e.g. a "which port to check for this game" resolver, or backoff/retry-count math) — check `test/` for the `npx tsx --test test/*.test.ts` convention already used in this repo.
- **Disk space discipline, this is important**: a disk-full incident happened on this exact host earlier today from multiple concurrent agents each installing a full real `node_modules` copy in worktrees that never got cleaned up. Before running `npm ci`, run `df -h /` and confirm there's at least 5GB free — if not, say so in your report rather than proceeding blindly. Give your worktree its own real `node_modules` via `npm ci` (not a symlink — a symlinked `node_modules` caused a separate real incident today, briefly corrupting production's generated Prisma client) but when you're done and have committed your work, **delete your worktree's `node_modules` and `.next` directories yourself before finishing** (`rm -rf node_modules .next` in the worktree) — the code is safe once committed to the branch; there's no reason to leave a multi-GB disposable build artifact sitting on disk after you're done. This is a new hard requirement for this task specifically, given today's incident.

## Build safety

`cd /opt/nxeon && git worktree add /opt/nxeon-wt-provhealth -b feature/provision-health-check`, symlink only `.env`, real `node_modules` via `npm ci`. `npm run build` and `npx tsc --noEmit` must pass clean, plus the test suite. This touches the core provisioning path for every future order (VPS and game) — meaningful risk. Commit your work but do NOT merge to main, do NOT touch staging or production. Stop after committing, clean up your own `node_modules`/`.next` as instructed above, and report back for review.

Report back: exactly what the health check does for each server type, how retries/backoff are tuned and why, the failure-path behavior (what a customer/admin would actually see if it fails), the commit hash, and confirmation you cleaned up your own disk usage before finishing.

Working tree is clean (no uncommitted changes), `main` in `/opt/nxeon` is untouched, and nothing was merged.

## Report

**What the health check does, per server type**

Inserted into `provision()` in `/opt/nxeon-wt-provhealth/worker/index.ts`, right after the guest-agent wait and before the `RUNNING` status flip / deployment email:

1. **Every server (VPS and game)**: a real TCP connect + wait for a genuine `SSH-2.0-...` banner (not just a completed handshake, since a closed port dropping the connection can look similar to a refusal). Target address reuses the function's existing `dedicated`/`sshPort`/`ip` variables exactly as the existing `sshLine` readiness message does: dedicated IP on port 22, or the NAT host's public IP + assigned `sshPort`. Retries every 5s for up to 2 minutes (24 attempts).

2. **Game servers only**: gated on resolving a known family from `server.osTemplate.family` (falls back through `gamePlan.gameFamily` if ever loaded) via a new `GAME_PORT` map added to `lib/games.ts`, covering all 19 `GAME_FAMILIES`, sourced directly from each game's real `docker run -p ...` mapping in `prisma/catalog.ts` / `seed-wave1-games.ts` / `seed-wave2-games.ts` (Terraria = 7777/tcp, matching the task's example). Several titles (valheim, palworld, vrising, enshrouded, theforest, sonsoftheforest, bedrock) expose only a UDP port in their image — no TCP port exists to check — so for those the map points at UDP and the check uses a connect+send UDP probe (an ICMP port-unreachable surfaces as `ECONNREFUSED` on Linux if nothing is bound, so this still catches "process never bound the port," just without TCP's certainty). Where an image exposes both, TCP is preferred. Retries every 10s for up to 5 minutes (30 attempts) — no real order was placed to time an actual boot (out of scope for a prod-adjacent branch), so this is a documented, principled default, not a measured one; the timeout/interval are named exports (`GAME_PORT_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS`/`_INTERVAL_MS`) for easy retuning once real data exists. Checked against `ip` (dedicated public IP, or the VM's private NAT address) rather than through the public NAT path, since NAT servers only get an automatic port-forward for SSH — the game's own port is forwarded only if a customer adds one — so checking the VM's own address is the only way to verify what the check exists to prove (the game process bound its port) independent of that separate, pre-existing gap.

**Failure path**: the check simply `throw`s an Error with a diagnostic message (`"SSH did not respond on H:P after ~Ns (N attempts; last error: ...)"` vs `"game port 7777/tcp never opened on IP after ~Ns ..."`), matching this codebase's established convention exactly — no new error-handling code was needed. The existing `runJob` catch path takes it from there: retries while `Job.attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS`, and on the terminal attempt flips `Server.status` to `ERROR`, calls the existing `cleanupFailedProvision()` (releases the dedicated IP / clears `ipAddress` per the established leak-prevention logic), and calls `notifyProvisionFailed()` (persists `provisionError`, in-app notification, and a "We couldn't set up X" email). Because the check runs before the `RUNNING` write and before `sendServerDeployedEmail`, neither ever fires on failure — and because it's a plain throw with no side effects of its own, a subsequent retry re-runs it cleanly, fitting the function's existing idempotent-retry design.
